extracted.intended_audience: scientists and prospective FRO founders, and potential philanthropic funders/intermediaries
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for submitting Focused Research Organization (FRO) ideas to Convergent Research, including what fits the FRO model, how proposals are evaluated, funding pathways, and expected outputs and safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission process and confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: We gladly accept FRO idea submissions at any time. Please use this form. We will not share your proposal outside Convergent Research without your permission, but please do not directly disclose confidential, unfiled IP in your proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit via the provided form; expect confidentiality but do not include unfiled or confidential IP in the initial submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal format and initial evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Our team initially evaluates incoming few-page proposals at a high level, with targeted outreach to domain experts and iterative follow-up conversations with the proposers as needed to ensure their idea is a potential fit for an FRO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a concise few-page proposal; be prepared for targeted expert outreach and iterative follow-up rather than an immediate detailed review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical roadmapping to identify bottlenecks
rubrics_metrics.description: We start by performing systematic technical roadmapping research to identify bottlenecks to progress in key scientific fields. This roadmapping takes the form of targeted investigations conducted with world-leading scientists, workshops to bring together diverse perspectives on the challenges facing specific scientific fields, fellowships and competitions for whitepapers, and other methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals that align with identified bottlenecks and the outputs of CR’s roadmapping activities are more likely to be considered; engagement in workshops, whitepapers, and fellowships can feed into proposal generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funder interest as a gating criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: We then assess whether there is potential interest from a funder in our network for the FRO idea. If a project has sufficient funder interest, we help the FRO founding team incubate the idea. Convergent Research does not fund FROs directly. We attempt to match proposed FROs and their founding teams with members of our network of potential funders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear path to funder interest (or an anchor donor) is effectively a precondition for incubation; proposals should consider and articulate potential funder alignment or demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensive technical proposal requirements (post-funder match)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a potential funder is identified for a proposed FRO, we guide the prospective FRO’s founding team in writing an extensive technical proposal, including defining the specific milestones they intend to achieve in their project and their plans for technology transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to develop a detailed proposal with explicit milestones and concrete technology transfer plans; expect extensive review and iteration with world experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Milestones and technology transfer clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals should define the specific milestones they intend to achieve in their project and their plans for technology transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail measurable milestones and explicit pathways for how outputs will be transferred, deployed, or otherwise used by the broader field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit-for-FRO necessity (anti-pattern: doable in academic lab)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Just do what my lab already does, but with more money." If a scientific project can be readily done in an academic lab, it should be done there! It is not worth the effort of setting up an entirely new nonprofit organization if doing so is not required to undertake a project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate why the work cannot be accomplished within existing academic institutions—FROs are for projects that require a different operating model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for capital- and team-intensive systems engineering
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects for which [an FRO] is required often involve hiring many engineers or other non-trainee talent at industry wages, or doing significant amounts of non-publishable work, both of which are hard in an academic lab.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your project requires large-scale, long-term team hiring, industrial pay scales, or non-publishable engineering/infrastructure work, it fits the kinds of activities suited to an FRO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: unstructured 'blue-sky' aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Hire 20 of the best researchers and let them work on blue-sky, individual projects in the same building." This does not take advantage of the multidisciplinary hiring opportunities or the startup-like organization structure that FROs afford.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals should articulate structured, coordinated team strategies that leverage multidisciplinary hiring and an organization design, not just aggregate star individuals working independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: repackaging a startup
rubrics_metrics.description: “Do my startup idea, just with nonprofit funding.” If a scientific project can be done as a startup (without severely curtailing or altering its mission) then it should be done as a startup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your project is commercially viable and readily pursued by venture capital, it is likely not an ideal FRO candidate; explain why nonprofit/philanthropic governance is the better choice if applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate project types: catalytic tool-building and infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: Many transformative projects in science, especially tool-building or infrastructure projects, are unglamorous and underrated. Many such projects are well-suited for FROs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize catalytic, enabling outputs (datasets, protocols, tools, distribution systems) that broadly accelerate a field rather than only chasing the 'white whale' scientific problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Societal risk assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Does Convergent Research assess FRO proposals for risks to society? Yes. We regularly consult with experts on specific risks, and have already ruled out incubating 3-4 potential FROs due to risk considerations (such as having too much downside potential alongside its potential benefits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals should include consideration of societal risks and mitigation strategies; high downside potential can disqualify an idea regardless of technical promise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain applicability beyond biology
rubrics_metrics.description: The FRO model is applicable to many fields of science. We are currently incubating FROs in climate measurement, mathematical theorem proving, materials science, and other areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While early FROs were biology-focused, proposers from diverse scientific domains are encouraged to apply if their project fits the model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctive structural characteristics of FROs
rubrics_metrics.description: ARPA-style programs coordinate distributed teams based at existing organizations, each working on their own sub-project, whereas each FRO is a new, dedicated organization, focusing on a single project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify why a new dedicated organization (rather than distributed grants or coordination) is necessary for achieving the project's goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected outputs and commitment to dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: A top priority for FROs is ensuring the results of their work are disseminated and used broadly across the scientific field of which they are a part... non-exhaustive list: release open-source or open-access datasets and protocols; distribute reagents or tools to researchers; publish research papers; publish educational resources, or host visitors and run workshops; integrate their technologies into larger projects; license IP to companies when necessary; spin out new entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals should specify intended outputs and concrete dissemination plans; the review process vets how researchers would use the FRO’s proposed outputs to transform their work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual property and commercialization policy
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases, public benefit will best be served by licensing technologies developed by the FRO to companies or by spinning off startups. Free use of FRO IP for research purposes by academics and non-profits will be preserved regardless of the commercialization plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline any intended commercialization/licensing/spinout strategy and explicitly preserve (or explain) access rights for academics and non-profits if applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Donor engagement tiers and typical uses of funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Gifts to Convergent Research can support FROs at three levels: At the $10M+ level, you can potentially anchor a new FRO... At the $1M+ level, you can join in funding an FRO that already has an anchor donor... At the $10k+ level, you can support our scientific roadmapping and FRO sourcing programs (e.g., ~$60k supports a workshop and whitepaper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Donors should consider what their contribution aims to enable (anchor/incubate, de-risking research, or roadmapping/sourcing) and structure gifts accordingly; small gifts can meaningfully support ideation activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incubation support from Convergent Research
rubrics_metrics.description: We guide the prospective FRO’s founding team in writing an extensive technical proposal... These proposals are extensively reviewed and improved, typically in collaboration with world experts in the relevant scientific fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Founding teams can expect active support in proposal development and expert review once funder interest exists; the process emphasizes iteration and expert-driven improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation about project duration and career paths
rubrics_metrics.description: FROs are finite-duration projects. During their later years they work to actively disseminate and deploy the public goods they create into the real world... We expect people who work at FROs to have many opportunities in industry and academia after the FRO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals and prospective team members should be aligned with a finite-duration, mission-focused organization and plan for later transition or scaling of outputs and staff careers.
